* **Open Source**: The entire platform code is available in public GitHub repositories for community contributions.
articles.decoder: * **MCP (Model Context Protocol)**: An open standard developed by Anthropic that allows AI agents to securely connect to external data sources and tools.

articles.title: AI-Powered Diagramming & Text-to-Chart Tool (Website)
articles.description: Prompt inside the canvas, drop in a doc, or write it in code, and watch the diagram build itself.
articles.one-liner: Mermaid AI adds natural language generation, real-time collaboration, and file ingestion to the popular open-source diagramming library.

summary.what: Building on Mermaid.js, this new platform allows users to generate diagrams from text prompts, transcripts, or documents, and features an MCP server for integration with Cursor, Claude, and VS Code.
summary.why: This transitions diagramming from a manual 'syntax-first' task to an AI-assisted workflow, keeping documentation in sync with evolving system architecture.
summary.takeaway: Connect the Mermaid MCP server to your AI IDE (like Cursor or VS Code) to generate diagrams directly from your codebase.

articles.deep-summary:
* **Workflow Integration**: Allows in-canvas prompting to adjust charts without manual syntax editing.
* **File Context**: Processes PDFs, PRDs, and transcripts to generate context-aware architecture or project flow diagrams.
* **Enterprise Features**: Includes SOC 2 compliance, SSO, and real-time co-editing capabilities.
* **Ecosystem**: Maintains compatibility with the underlying Mermaid.js open-source syntax.
articles.decoder:
* **Mermaid.js**: An open-source JavaScript-based diagramming tool that renders text/markdown definitions into SVG diagrams.
* **Sequence Diagram**: A type of diagram that shows how objects operate with one another and in what order.

articles.title: This beautiful logo design was created to grow like nature
articles.description: Philadelphia-based Smith & Diction has redesigned the Pennsylvania Horticultural Society's identity ahead of its 200th anniversary, replacing a generic tree emblem with a dynamic representation of plant life. The new PHS lettermark acts as a root system from which different native plants grow, with illustrations by Summer McClure arranged within rectangles inspired by Philadelphia's street grid. Frame-by-frame animations by Henrique Barone depict plants growing from the letterforms, while additional animations and a printed flipbook bring the identity's organic movement to life.
articles.one-liner: Smith & Diction designed a dynamic, root-inspired identity for the Pennsylvania Horticultural Society using frame-by-frame animation to mimic organic growth.

summary.what: The agency rebranded the 200-year-old institution by replacing a static tree logo with a lettermark that serves as a base for custom native plant illustrations.
summary.why: The project serves as a case study for modern identity systems that utilize generative or multi-state assets (animations, flipbooks, and user-contributed illustrations) to feel 'alive' rather than static.

articles.deep-summary:
* **System Design**: The logo uses a modular approach where different plant illustrations can be swapped for specific sub-brands (e.g., flower shows).
* **Technical Execution**: Hand-drawn frame-by-frame animations by Henrique Barone capture natural growth patterns.
* **Tangible Identity**: Includes a physical brand book, flipbook, and lapel pins, emphasizing the tactile nature of horticultural work.

articles.title: How Material Constraints Sharpen Design Thinking for Physical Projects
articles.description: Budget, environment, and lifespan give designers concrete criteria for revisiting choices made on screen before anything goes to production. Pentagram's bronze drain covers, PUMA's Clever Little Bag with 65% less cardboard than a shoebox, and the Eames plywood chair show constraints shaping form. Full-size samples, each testing one defined question, settle what flat layouts and renderings leave open.
articles.one-liner: Material constraints—budget, environment, and lifespan—act as objective filters that sharpen design decisions before a project moves to production.

summary.what: Eleanor Hecks argues that designers should treat physical limitations as a 'creative brief' rather than hurdles, using examples like PUMA’s cardboard-efficient shoe packaging.
summary.why: Digital design often lacks feedback on material failure points (e.g., outdoor light reflection or physical folding stress), so prototype testing is the only way to validate screen-based choices.
summary.takeaway: Build a full-size prototype for every project and define one specific question it must answer before moving to mass production.

articles.deep-summary:
* **Physical Reality**: Flat digital renderings rarely account for environmental variables like sun glare or material degradation.
* **Test Protocols**: Change only one variable per prototype (e.g., stock type or joint design) to isolate cause-and-effect.
* **Constraints as Criteria**: Use maintenance requirements (e.g., graffiti resistance, cleanability) to narrow down material choices early in the brief.
articles.decoder: * **Substrate**: The underlying material or surface (like metal, plastic, or paper) onto which an image or text is printed.

articles.title: Lighting That Feels Just Right
articles.description: Real-time global illumination supplies what simple Blinn-Phong lighting lacks: light that bounces, bleeds color, and tints neighboring surfaces. Screen-Space Global Illumination comes first, followed by a more practical probe-based approach to estimating indirect light in browser-based 3D scenes. Reflections, sky light, volumetric lighting, and atmospheric scattering are then layered on for the finished look.
articles.one-liner: Maxime Heckel details the implementation of probe-based Global Illumination in the browser to add color bleeding and indirect light to 3D scenes.

summary.what: The article walks through moving from screen-space approximations to a more stable probe-based system that uses compute shaders to capture light data in world space.
summary.why: Indirect lighting is the missing piece for high-fidelity browser 3D; probe-based methods allow for stable light bounces that persist even when the camera moves or off-screen objects interact.
summary.takeaway: If you are working with Three.js, review their native probe-based GI implementation for a production-grade alternative to the custom code presented here.

articles.deep-summary:
* **Screen-Space vs. Probe-Based**: Screen-space GI fails for off-camera objects; probes solve this by pre-computing light in 3D grid volumes.
* **Temporal Accumulation**: Uses history textures and hysteresis to blend results over time, reducing noise without the massive performance cost of full path tracing.
* **Sky Light**: Incorporates atmospheric scattering to provide a natural environmental tint to the indirect light.
* **Reflections**: Uses ray-traced reflection rays against the probe atlas to simulate complex light bounces on shiny surfaces.
* **Compute Shaders**: Leverages WebGPU-like TSL (Three.js Shading Language) to handle the compute-heavy tasks of updating probe light estimations.
articles.decoder:
* **Global Illumination (GI)**: A set of techniques that simulate how light bounces off surfaces to illuminate other objects, rather than just calculating direct light from sources.
* **Path Tracing**: An algorithm that simulates light paths to create realistic images, computationally expensive but visually accurate.
* **Hysteresis**: A process where the current state depends on past values; here, it controls the blend ratio between new light samples and historical data to prevent flickering.
* **Schlick Fresnel**: An approximation used to calculate how much light is reflected off a surface based on the viewing angle; essential for realistic material look.

articles.title: Font vs typeface: the ultimate guide
articles.description: A typeface describes a shared visual design across a family of characters, while a font traditionally refers to a particular weight, width, and style or its corresponding digital file, although variable fonts have blurred this distinction by combining multiple styles within a single file.
articles.one-liner: Variable fonts have effectively dismantled the traditional distinction between a font and a typeface by consolidating entire families into a single file.

summary.what: A typeface is a cohesive visual design family, while a font is a specific instance (weight/style) or digital file. Variable fonts, introduced via OpenType in 2016, use sliders to modify parameters like weight and width within one file, blurring these historic definitions.
summary.why: The rise of digital distribution and variable font technology makes traditional distinctions based on physical metal type sets largely obsolete, shifting the focus from 'collections of files' to 'tunable parameters.'

articles.deep-summary:
* A typeface refers to the overarching aesthetic family (e.g., Helvetica).
* A font refers to the specific weight/style iteration or the digital file itself.
* Metal type history defined 'founts' as sets of physical lead characters.
* Variable fonts use axes (weight, width, optical size) to provide infinite variations in one file.
* CSS uses 'font-family' for the typeface and 'font-weight' for specific variants, complicating the nomenclature.
articles.decoder:
* **Variable font**: An OpenType font format that allows multiple styles and weights to be stored within a single file, adjustable via continuous axes rather than discrete static files.
* **Optical size**: A design feature that adjusts the stroke thickness and spacing of characters based on the intended display size to improve readability.
* **X-height**: The height of lowercase letters, excluding ascenders (like 'h') and descenders (like 'p'), which impacts legibility.
